description_en: Ajayamerukoṭa is situated 4 km north-west of Amargaḍhī, the Dadeldhura district headquarters. Most of the monuments are built on the right bank of the Chaurī Gāḍ river, an affluent of the Mahakali (or Sharda) river, that makes the western river between India and Nepal. The monument is located in an area where are found other contemporary constructions (DDL0110,DDL0111,DDL0112,DDL0113andDDL0120).The area of Ajayamerukoṭa is rich in monuments that were mostly erected during the 14th and 15th centuries. According to D. P. Ojha, Ajayamerukoṭa was a local capital of the Khasiya kings from Jumla, (i.e. the Khaśa Malla emperors, 12th-14th century) (Ojha 1989: p. 54). From the mid-14th century, Ajayamerukoṭa seems to have taken greater importance as a capital of the Doti kingdom, especially under the reign of king Niraya Pāla (r. c. 1362-1383 AD). Indeed, it is around Niraya Pāla's time that Doti emerged as an entity independant from the Khaśa Malla empire. This political and economical rise is demonstrated in the numerous monuments erected between the second half of the 14th century and throughout the 15th century.Stone pillars were erected throughout the Karnali Basin from the 13th to the 17th century. They are installed to honor the memory of deceased persons, mostly warriors.The pillar is located four meters south-east from theśikharatempleDDL0133. Its iconography is very similar to that of a pillar located next to a nearby pavilion (bhaiṭak,DDL0120-001). The four sides of the pillar are adorned by carved reliefs. To the south are foliages, a couple of affronted horned animals and a horse rider. To the west is a couple of intertwined snakes, a lion or a tiger seemingly hunting a quadruped. On top is a scene with a central male character seated in the noble attitude (Skt.sattvaparyaṅka). His hands are resting on the knees, in the gesture of knowledge (Skt.jñānamudrā). Prayag Raj Sharma's interpretation of this character as a Buddha appears inacurrate considering its iconography, not matching that of Buddhas (Sharma 2012, p. 299). One female character is standing on each side of the seated figure.On the north side are foliages, a couple of affronted horned animals, topped by an image of the god Sūrya standing and holding a lotus in both hands. On the east side is a couple of intertwined snakes, a couple of affronted birds and a scene with a horserider raising a sword in its left hand. To the left of the rider is a standing (female?) character with its hands joined in front of its belly. One or two lines of text are inscribed in Nāgarī script on each sides of the pillar. According to P. R. Sharma the inscription is dated of ŚS 1309 (1387 AD) and 'indicates to have been the memorial of Kālu Sutāhār during the time of Nāga Malla. However, the whole inscription is otherwise illegible.' (Sharma 2012, p. 299).A fence of barbed wires was installed around the pillar when it was surveyed in 2015.
monument_assessment: Slightly damaged (minor damages such as minor cracks, plants, missing stones in plinths), Surface damages
references: REFERENCES Ojha, D. P. 1988. Doti Kṣetrako Itihās tathā Saṃnskrīti . Kathmandu: Sudur Paścimāncal Sāmājik Sevā tathā Anusandhān Samiti. Sharma, Dilli Raj. 2012. Heritage of Western Nepal. Art and Architecture . Kathmandu: Centre for Nepal and Asian Studies, pp. 296-299.
